rows.practice: develops design proposals of moderate complexity through iterative drawing and modelling, answering a brief with attention to site, materials and technical coherence
rows.knowledge: construction systems, building physics, fire and life safety, climate and regenerative design principles and the cultural and historical precedents that shape buildings
rows.identity: an architecture student who follows professional codes of conduct and weighs the ethical effects of design on society, the environment and wellbeing

rows.practice: uses architectural research methods and digital tools to test design decisions, then presents and defends the proposal to clients, reviewers and lay audiences
rows.knowledge: the legal and commercial framework of building projects, from procurement and contracts to planning systems, cost control and the economic forces that shape a scheme
rows.identity: a designer who listens to and works with the people a building serves and treats equity, inclusion and accessibility as design obligations

rows.practice: resolves complex proposals with originality and systems thinking, applying chosen research methods and BIM, computational design and fabrication to evolve a considered architectural language
rows.knowledge: global architectural history and theory read through narratives and values, alongside social and climate justice and how to apply regenerative principles to real projects
rows.identity: an architect in formation who advocates for communities, accepts civic duty and climate justice and regulates own conduct when building collaborative design teams

digest.definition: Architecture joins the arts, sciences and humanities, combining creative and analytical approaches to the challenges of built and natural environments; architects act as communicators, coordinators and advocates
distinctiveFeatures: Architecture joins the arts, sciences and humanities, combining creative and analytical approaches to the challenges of built and natural environments; architects act as communicators, coordinators and advocates
Design, broadly understood, is the defining skill: a method, a creative act, a technical discipline and a cultural practice
Design is contested, so the discipline advances by critique and asks students to live with the unknown and the unfinished
Work is collaborative and leads towards shared authorship and leadership of mixed teams
It is professionally oriented, with most courses validated or accredited, yet its learning transfers to many other careers
Teaching centres on the studio as space, method and culture, with project-based learning and reviews
The statement frames the subject through twelve overlapping literacies that support an ethos of intelligent generalism

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: a profession seeking a more representative graduate body; inclusive studio culture and diverse voices; a decolonising rereading of history and theory; the hidden costs of materials, kit, trips and long studio hours; the strain of reviews (D1, 1.6 to 1.11, 3.33, 3.36, 3.37)

legal duties for adjustments, with the subject's own expertise in accessible design as a reason to go further; neurodivergent students in the studio environment; flexible assessment and alternatives to in-person review (D1, 1.12 to 1.18, 2.15, 3.34)

the climate and ecological emergency as a call for rapid change; climate literacy built across the course; regenerative design, whole life carbon and predictive tools; a critical stance on sustainability itself; providers leading by example (D1, 1.19 to 1.25, 3.33)
named as employability, entrepreneurship and enterprise education: career readiness, placements, live projects, alumni networks and careers beyond the title of architect (D1, 1.26 to 1.35, 3.41)

a fifth cross-cutting theme in this statement: GenAI in industry and its ethical, IP, data and bias issues; authorship and process in assessment; use policies; inclusive and affordable use (D1, 1.36 to 1.40, 3.40)

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Architecture degree

statements.about: governance differences across the nations
statements.paraphrase: Architecture is a professionally oriented, global field that most students enter hoping to become architects, though many move to other careers; courses should allow for how governance, law, policy and practice vary, as fits each course's focus.

forPractitioner.text: Build the national and devolved differences in governance, law, policy and practice that suit your course's focus into what students learn, since many will work across borders.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: a sustained provider commitment to EDI
statements.paraphrase: The profession needs a graduate body that better reflects the society it designs for, and barriers to entry persist; providers must keep developing a sustained, reflective commitment to equity, diversity and inclusion, which should be built into the culture and practice of architectural education.

forPractitioner.text: Treat equity, diversity and inclusion as a standing commitment of the provider, reviewed and renewed over time, and make it part of how the school teaches, assesses and engages with the profession, not a separate initiative.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: reflective processes for equity and inclusive curricula
statements.paraphrase: Inclusive settings value what each person brings; schools should set up continuing reflective processes to tackle new equity and diversity issues and work with students on more inclusive curricula and teaching, and providers carry a duty to keep widening fair access and opportunity.

forPractitioner.text: Set up a standing, reflective process for spotting and acting on equity and diversity issues, co-design more inclusive curricula and teaching with students and keep improving fair access so every student can progress.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: a respectful studio culture with diverse voices
statements.paraphrase: Schools should keep the learning environment inclusive, supportive and respectful, open to critique of established approaches, and where they can should bring students into contact with a wide range of voices and perspectives, from staff, guest speakers, reviewers and consultants.

forPractitioner.text: Keep the studio and wider learning environment inclusive and respectful while open to challenging established views, and widen the range of people students hear from: staff, visiting speakers, reviewers and consultants from inside and outside the field.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: the hidden costs of study
statements.paraphrase: Extra visible and hidden costs, such as materials, hardware, software, study visits and long studio hours, can exclude students; schools should recognise these effects, try to keep extra costs down and support fair access to resources and should also recognise unequal access to work-based learning.

forPractitioner.text: Audit what students pay beyond fees (materials, kit, software, trips) and the time studio culture demands, cut those costs where you can, back fair access to resources and watch for students shut out of work-based learning or practice experience.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: the strain of presenting work in reviews
statements.paraphrase: Studio learning means students often present work to others, which some find hard; schools should recognise the particular difficulties reviews can bring, and programmes can use a variety of modes and methods to support inclusive learning.

forPractitioner.text: Recognise that presenting in reviews is hard for some students, and use varied modes and methods of delivery and assessment, perhaps with an inclusive curriculum toolkit, so the studio supports different learners.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: legal duties to make reasonable adjustments
statements.paraphrase: Institutions are bound by law, under the Equality Act 2010 and the earlier Disability Discrimination Act 1995 and Education Act 1996, to provide reasonable adjustments for students and staff; schools of architecture, often expert in accessible design, are well placed to go further.

forPractitioner.text: Meet the legal duty to make reasonable adjustments (the Equality Act 2010, with the 1995 and 1996 Acts the paragraph also names), and use the school's own expertise in accessible design to go beyond those adjustments.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: holistic approaches to accessibility
statements.paraphrase: Institutions should take integrated, whole approaches to accessibility that support success, moving past basic compliance towards environments where all students and staff thrive, a duty the subject carries with special weight given its commitment to inclusive design.

forPractitioner.text: Take an integrated, whole-school approach to accessibility that goes past compliance; because the discipline teaches inclusive design, its own spaces and curriculum should model it.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: oversight frameworks for conflicting needs in groups
statements.paraphrase: Different individual needs in a group can conflict; providers should therefore develop clear oversight frameworks for fair, open decisions in such cases, which also helps teach emotional literacy to students of every neurotype.

forPractitioner.text: Set up a clear framework for deciding fairly and openly when students' needs clash within group work, and use it as a chance to build emotional literacy across the cohort.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: reasonable adjustments to the physical studio
statements.paraphrase: The physical setting matters for neurodivergent students, who spend long periods in studio, where lighting, acoustics, clutter and a lack of breakout space can be disabling; course teams should consider reasonable adjustments to physical settings that harm disabled students.

forPractitioner.text: Look at the studio as a working environment for neurodivergent and disabled students (light, sound, clutter, places to step away) and consider reasonable adjustments where it disadvantages them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: critical engagement with sustainability
statements.paraphrase: Sustainability in architecture is broad, complex and changing, so curricula should give students room to examine the idea critically, including its limits and new alternative approaches.

forPractitioner.text: Give students room in the curriculum to question sustainability itself, its limits and emerging alternatives, rather than presenting it as a settled checklist.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.appliesTo: courses in the subject and their students
statements.about: climate literacy built across the course
statements.paraphrase: Grounding in climate literacy, competence and capability will be developed across the creative, cultural, technical and professional sides of the subject, helped by real-world applications and by predictive tools that test design decisions.

forPractitioner.text: Develop climate literacy across every strand of the course, not in one module: tie it to real-world application and bring in predictive tools, for example energy or performance modelling and whole life carbon checks, to test design choices.

forBeneficiary.text: You will build a solid grounding in climate literacy across every part of your studies, from design and culture to technology and practice, and you may use tools such as energy modelling to test your design choices.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: providers modelling sustainable practice
statements.paraphrase: Providers should try to lead by example, reviewing and improving their sustainability education practice with their students; modelling environmental and ethical practice lets schools encourage students to do the same at work and at home.

forPractitioner.text: Model the environmental and ethical practice you teach, and review and refine your sustainability education with your students on a continuing basis.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: fair support in finding placements
statements.paraphrase: Placements, defined as credit-rated periods of practice work within an undergraduate or master's course, carry an ethical duty on schools to protect students from poor working practice, and providers should try to give every student equal support in finding one.

forPractitioner.text: Where placements are offered, protect students from poor working practices during them, and make sure every student gets the same level of help in securing a placement.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: risk and ethics in live projects
statements.paraphrase: Live projects in the core curriculum ground learning in real challenges and support enterprise; those involving field trips and community work will need to deal with risk, ethical implications and accessibility for students.

forPractitioner.text: When you run live projects with field trips or community engagement, plan for risk, ethics and student accessibility from the outset.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: teaching about GenAI and its implications
statements.paraphrase: Architecture education will need to cover how GenAI is used in industry, which should include its ethical, sustainability, intellectual property and data protection implications, bias in models and ways to reduce it; providers should attend to students' critical judgement of GenAI outputs and their ability to explain how they prompted and refined the tools.

forPractitioner.text: Teach how industry uses GenAI and its ethical, environmental, intellectual property and data protection implications, including bias and its mitigation, and build students' critical judgement of outputs and their ability to account for how they used the tools.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the curriculum; the student-facing outcome is in the digital literacy items 4.6.b6 and 4.7.b6

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: research-informed methods in studio assessment
statements.paraphrase: Critical and reflective assessment can expose design authorship and process, with GenAI used as an aid to exploration rather than an end; courses should keep encouraging speculative, analytical, research-informed and novel ways of working in studio design assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Use critical and reflective assessment to make authorship and process visible, treat GenAI as a facilitating tool and keep valuing speculative, analytical and research-informed methods in design assessment.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Architecture degree

statements.about: inclusive and affordable use of GenAI
statements.paraphrase: Providers should make sure GenAI is introduced in a way that promotes inclusion rather than amplifying privilege, weighing the teaching needed and the cost to students before requiring specialist tools for compulsory work.

forPractitioner.text: Before a brief requires a specialist GenAI tool, consider what teaching students need to use it and what it costs them, so the tool widens inclusion rather than rewarding those who can pay.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: a curriculum open to emerging knowledge
statements.paraphrase: Curriculum design should stay flexible enough to take in new knowledge and techniques, such as regulatory change, digital fabrication, sustainable methods and artificial intelligence, so students meet the subject as both an academic discipline and a fast-changing profession.

forPractitioner.text: Keep the curriculum flexible enough to absorb new knowledge and techniques (regulation, fabrication, sustainable methods, AI) so students see the field as an academic discipline and as a profession in rapid change.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: research and creativity for varied careers
statements.paraphrase: The education builds in lifelong learning and professional development, and since courses often prepare students for varied careers or further study, course design should instil the research and creativity that support those and new routes, with transferable skills made visible to students.

forPractitioner.text: Design the course to build research and creativity that serve registration and other careers or further study alike, and make the hard and soft transferable skills explicit to students.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.appliesTo: undergraduates on combined or joint degrees
statements.about: core threshold standards in joint and combined degrees
statements.paraphrase: Undergraduates taking architecture in a combined or joint degree will reach the core elements of the threshold standards here and will add others from the areas their other subject covers.

forPractitioner.text: In a joint or combined degree, students will meet the core elements of the threshold literacies and add others drawn from their second subject; design the joint curriculum so both hold.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study architecture as part of a joint or combined degree, you will reach the core parts of the minimum literacies for the subject and add others from your second subject.

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: PSRB content requirements and wider experience
statements.paraphrase: In designing courses, providers should take account of what the professional bodies, chiefly ARB and RIBA, require as minimum content, while giving a broad education that encourages experiment, critical investigation and intellectual growth past mere compliance.

forPractitioner.text: Map the ARB and RIBA minimum content requirements into the modules, then design beyond them so students experiment, investigate critically and grow intellectually rather than just comply.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: monitoring practice and study abroad; adjustments
statements.paraphrase: Practical experience or study abroad within a course should be properly monitored by the provider, progression routes should consider individual needs and reasonable adjustments should, where fitting, align each student's experience with equitable and inclusive measures.

forPractitioner.text: Monitor placements and study abroad that sit within the course, shape progression routes around individual needs and put reasonable adjustments in place so time away is equitable and inclusive.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: apprenticeship routes to the subject
statements.paraphrase: Apprenticeships at Level 7 (Architect) and Level 6 (Architectural Assistant) now offer integrated routes to RIBA-validated Part 2 and 3 or Part 1 courses; providers should consult the national trailblazer groups' requirements when exploring them.

forPractitioner.text: If you offer or plan the Level 6 or Level 7 architecture apprenticeships, work from the relevant national trailblazer groups' requirements alongside RIBA validation.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: inclusive and accessible course design
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be designed with inclusion and accessibility in mind, and institutions may offer varied modes and routes, full-time, part-time, in-person or blended, to widen access.

forPractitioner.text: Design every course for inclusion and accessibility from the start, and consider whether full-time, part-time, campus studio or blended and online modes would widen access.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: consistent quality and standards in partnerships
statements.paraphrase: Providers may deliver through national or international partnerships, including franchise, validation, articulation and transnational arrangements; when they do they must ensure the quality and standards of the degree stay consistent and that every student, wherever based, reaches the standards this statement sets.

forPractitioner.text: In any franchise, validation, articulation or transnational partnership, make sure the quality and standards of the architecture degree are the same everywhere and that every student, wherever they study, meets these standards.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: applying the standards across partnered awards
statements.paraphrase: Partnerships range from formal joint delivery to looser arrangements; in all of them the statement and its standards should be applied so that a partnered award reaches the expected outcomes across the whole programme.

forPractitioner.text: Apply these standards to the whole of any qualification involving partners, formal or informal, so the outcomes hold across every part of the programme.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: external reviewers in periodic review
statements.paraphrase: Externality is central to UK quality assurance: providers will use external reviewers in periodic review for an independent view on changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Bring in external reviewers for periodic review to test proposed changes independently and confirm that threshold standards are met and content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of the Architecture course

statements.about: the cross-cutting themes in design, content and delivery
statements.paraphrase: Monitoring and review can make sure the cross-cutting themes run through the curriculum; programmes should reflect them in design, content and delivery, and reviews are the chance to judge how well they are woven in.

forPractitioner.text: Reflect the cross-cutting themes (equity and inclusion, accessibility, sustainability, enterprise, GenAI) in course design, content and delivery, and use programme review to test how well they are woven through.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: the taxonomy of literacies and those who use it
statements.about: reading the literacies as overlapping
statements.paraphrase: The taxonomy offers a thematic frame linking professional body requirements to learning, teaching and assessment; the literacies should be read as interdependent and overlapping rather than discrete, and they help communication with non-specialists.

forPractitioner.text: Use the twelve literacies as an overlapping frame that links professional requirements to teaching and assessment, not as separate boxes to tick module by module.

forBeneficiary.text: You will meet the twelve literacies as overlapping parts of one way of thinking about architecture, not as separate subjects, and they give you words to explain your work to people outside the field.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of a course in the subject
statements.about: the twelve literacies named
statements.paraphrase: On completing a course, a graduate is expected to have gained twelve literacies: design; visual and spatial; cultural and contextual; climate and ecological; technical and building environment; digital; research and enquiry; ethical and professional; practice and business; financial and economic; emotional; and communication.

forPractitioner.text: Plan the course so graduates acquire all twelve literacies, which 4.6 defines for honours and 4.7 for the master's; this paragraph only names them.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your course you will have built twelve literacies: design, visual and spatial, cultural and contextual, climate and ecological, technical, digital, research, ethical and professional, practice and business, financial, emotional and communication.

statements.about: portfolios showing process and outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Studio supports an iterative, reflective cycle of drawing and modelling in which experiment, risk and failure belong to the process; portfolios for assessment should show both the process and the results of studio projects.

forPractitioner.text: Ask for portfolios that show how a design developed, including tests and failures, as well as the finished outcome.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: studio facilities students need
statements.paraphrase: A studio needs good light and room for large models, and students need digital tools used across industry; ideally they should easily reach large-format printing and making facilities, and they should be able to store belongings and work securely, with digital substitutes where a physical studio is impossible.

forPractitioner.text: Provide a well-lit studio with space for large models, the digital tools industry uses, power and Wi-Fi, ready access to large-format printing and making facilities and secure storage; where physical studio space is not possible, replicate its features digitally.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: environmental and EDI effects of study visits
statements.paraphrase: Context is fundamental to studying architecture, and site and study visits offer contrasting settings, but programmes should keep in mind the environmental impact of flying and that long visits may be unaffordable or exclude students with outside commitments.

forPractitioner.text: Plan site and study visits with their environmental cost, especially air travel, and their affordability and fit with caring or work commitments in mind.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: non-visual and non-verbal alternatives to reviews
statements.paraphrase: Reviews give immediate feedback and build students' confidence to present to new audiences; providers will need to make sure non-visual and non-verbal alternatives are available as other forms of learning and assessment where needed.

forPractitioner.text: Run reviews as feedback and practice in presenting, and make sure non-visual and non-verbal alternatives exist for students who need them, both in learning and in assessment.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: staff preparation for inclusive reviews
statements.paraphrase: Student-centred review formats, such as grouped presentations, peer-led discussion with written feedback, changed layouts and online platforms, can respect diversity and access; schools should make sure staff have thought through review format and scope and been guided to support an inclusive environment.

forPractitioner.text: Brief and guide staff so they have considered the format and scope of each review, and try student-centred formats such as grouped presentations, peer discussion with written feedback and online reviews.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: reviews in summative assessment
statements.paraphrase: Where reviews count towards summative assessment, care should be taken that no individual or group is disadvantaged; since in-person presentation can unduly affect some students, alternative assessment will need to be considered, and providers are recommended to guide educators on inclusive feedback.

forPractitioner.text: If a review is summative, check that no student or group is disadvantaged, offer an alternative where in-person presentation would unfairly affect someone, and give staff guidance on inclusive, supportive feedback.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: guidance for external panel members
statements.paraphrase: Courses can use many kinds of assessment task, and capturing the design process matters more as Generative AI spreads; care should be taken that external panel members are guided on conduct and feedback in reviews so the environment stays inclusive.

forPractitioner.text: Use a range of assessment tasks that capture the design process (logbooks, decision rationales, reflective commentary), and brief external panel members on how to conduct reviews and give feedback inclusively.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: alternative assessment spaces
statements.paraphrase: The space and set-up for any assessment should suit architectural work and all students; alternative spaces, such as a recorded presentation or a quiet room, should be offered where needed, and most courses will need studio space for collective assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Set up assessment spaces that suit architectural work and every student, offer alternatives such as a recorded presentation or quiet room where needed and reserve studio space for physical submissions.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: students and those who teach them
statements.about: taking up group working
statements.paraphrase: Group working is integral to architectural practice and valuable in the curriculum; students should be encouraged to use group work when offered, and assessment can combine collective and individual contributions with reflection on feedback from group work.

forPractitioner.text: Encourage students to take up group projects when offered, and assess both the collective and the individual contribution, including the student's reflection on group feedback.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be encouraged to take part in group projects when they are on offer, because team working is central to architectural practice, and you may be assessed on both your shared and your own contribution.

statements.about: the minimum standards and the integrated master's route
statements.paraphrase: The statement sets minimum standards, as literacies, that a student will have shown when awarded an honours or a master's degree in architecture; an integrated master's student will have met the honours requirements before completing a year or its credit at FHEQ Level 7 or FQHEIS Level 11.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the literacies as the minimum every student will have demonstrated at award; for an integrated master's, students meet the honours minimum first, then complete a further year (or equivalent credit) at Level 7 or SCQF Level 11.

forBeneficiary.text: When you are awarded your degree, you will have shown at least the minimum level in each of the subject's literacies; on an integrated master's, you first reach the honours minimum and then complete a further year at master's level.

statements.about: evidence of achievement above the minimum
statements.paraphrase: Most students will perform well above the minimum; each provider sets its own way of judging evidence of this and should refer to Annex D of the Frameworks, which describes the four honours classifications.

forPractitioner.text: Judge achievement above the minimum by your own method, but anchor it to Annex D's descriptions of first, upper second, lower second and third-class honours.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: competence standards and EHRC guidance
statements.paraphrase: The minimum standards are not universal competence standards; a provider that develops competence standards under the Equality Act 2010 may draw on the statement and PSRB requirements and should follow the latest Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance.

forPractitioner.text: Do not treat the literacies as competence standards in the Equality Act sense; if you write competence standards for a programme specification, draw on the statement and PSRB requirements and follow current Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.about: PSRB outcomes for recognised degrees
statements.paraphrase: Many architecture degrees are recognised by ARB and RIBA; for those degrees, the themes, values, attributes and outcomes the bodies define for professional registration will apply.

forPractitioner.text: If your degree is recognised by ARB or RIBA, their themes, values, attributes and outcomes apply alongside these literacies; plan for both.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course or provider; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: conceiving and developing design proposals
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to conceive and develop architectural proposals of moderate complexity through an iterative process that brings together spatial, artistic, aesthetic, environmental and technical concerns, thinking critically and creatively and answering a brief with sensitivity to context and technical coherence.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will be able to take a design proposal of moderate complexity from idea to developed scheme, iterating and combining spatial, aesthetic, environmental and technical concerns, and answer a brief with technical coherence and regard for context.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will be able to come up with and develop a design of moderate complexity, working through it in cycles and pulling together space, art, environment and technical needs, so that it answers the brief and fits its setting.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: working with spatial and visual information
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to conceive, read, shape and convey spatial and visual information in drawings and models so that a coherent design develops, covering spatial relationships and how materials come together.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will be able to create, interpret, manipulate and communicate spatial and visual information in drawings and models to develop a coherent proposal, including spatial relationships and material assemblies.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will be able to imagine, read, work on and share spatial and visual ideas through drawings and models, using them to develop a coherent design that shows how spaces relate and how materials fit together.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: the cultural and historical contexts of architecture
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to understand and engage critically with the cultural, historical, theoretical, artistic and social settings that shape architecture, analysing precedents to inform design, grounded in history and theory drawn from many cultures, places and periods.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will understand, and engage critically with, the settings that shape architecture (cultural, historical, theoretical, artistic and social), analyse precedents to inform design and draw on history and theory from a range of global cultures and periods.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will understand and think critically about the cultural, historical, theoretical, artistic and social forces that shape buildings and use precedents from many cultures and periods to inform your designs.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: principles of climate change and regenerative design
statements.paraphrase: Will know the principles of climate change, loss of biodiversity, environmental impact and regenerative design strategies, including why responsible specification of materials, energy efficiency and ethical sourcing matter.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will know the principles behind climate change, the loss of biodiversity, environmental impact and regenerative design, and why responsible material specification, energy efficiency and ethical sourcing matter.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will know the main principles of climate change, biodiversity loss and environmental impact, the strategies of regenerative design and why choosing materials responsibly, saving energy and sourcing ethically matter.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: construction, building physics and life safety
statements.paraphrase: Will know construction systems, building physics and pathology, materials and environmental technologies and how to use them in quantitative and qualitative design work, including the principles of protecting life, fire safety, access and inclusive design, so as to integrate strategies that meet suitable performance standards.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will know construction systems, building physics, pathology, materials and environmental technologies, as well as the principles of life and fire safety, accessibility and inclusive design; they will integrate strategies that meet suitable performance standards in new build, reuse or conservation.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will know how buildings are built and how they perform (structure, materials, physics, decay and environmental systems), the basics of life safety, fire safety, access and inclusive design and how to build these into a design that performs as it should.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: digital tools and awareness of GenAI
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to use digital tools and technologies to design, evaluate and communicate architecture, and will be aware of how Generative artificial intelligence can be used in practice.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will be able to use digital tools in design, evaluation and communication and will be aware of the uses of generative AI in practice.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will be able to use digital tools to design, test and present your work, and you will know how generative AI can be used in architectural practice.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: research methods in architecture
statements.paraphrase: Will understand the research methods of architecture and how they support decisions informed by innovation and the growth of the discipline's knowledge.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will understand architectural research methods and how they support innovation-led decisions and advance knowledge in the field.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will understand how research is done in architecture and how it helps you make well-founded, innovative design decisions.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: codes of conduct and the ethics of design decisions
statements.paraphrase: Will know professional codes of conduct and the principles of equity, diversity, inclusion and accessibility, and understand the ethical effects of design decisions on society, the environment and wellbeing.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will know the profession's codes of conduct and the principles of equity, diversity, inclusion and accessibility, and understand how design decisions bear ethically on people, environment and wellbeing.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will know the codes of conduct architects follow and the principles of fairness, inclusion and access, and you will understand how design choices affect society, the environment and people's wellbeing.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: the professional, legal and business context
statements.paraphrase: Will know the principles of the professional, legal and business setting of architecture, including managing projects, procurement and contracts, policy, financial planning and cost control, planning systems, building codes and compliance with regulation.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will know the principles of architecture's professional, legal and business context: project management, procurement, contracts, policy, financial planning, cost management, planning, building codes and regulation.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will know the basics of how architecture works as a profession and a business, including managing projects, procurement, contracts, policy, budgets, the planning system, building regulations and compliance.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: financial and economic forces on projects
statements.paraphrase: Will be aware of how financial and economic mechanisms, local and global, shape and affect design proposals and how long a project lasts.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will be aware of how local and global financial and economic forces influence design proposals and the longevity of projects.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will be aware of how money and economics, close to home and worldwide, shape design proposals and how long buildings last.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: understanding and working with others when designing for them
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to understand, read and work with other people in order to design for someone else.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will be able to understand, interpret and collaborate with others in order to design for other people.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will be able to understand other people, read what they need and work with them so that you can design for them.

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the bachelor's degree with honours
statements.about: communicating ideas to varied audiences
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to put architectural ideas across clearly and effectively by spoken or other means, in writing and visually, presenting to varied audiences and producing coherent documents that support critical thinking and design intent.

forPractitioner.text: Every honours graduate will be able to communicate architectural ideas clearly and effectively in verbal or non-verbal, written and visual forms, present to diverse audiences and produce coherent documentation of design intent.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree, at minimum, you will be able to explain your architectural ideas clearly in speech or other forms, in writing and visually, present to different audiences such as clients and collaborators and produce clear documents that show your thinking and design intent.

statements.about: resolving complex design proposals
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to conceive, develop and resolve complex architectural proposals through a deliberate process and method that brings together spatial, artistic, aesthetic, environmental and technical concerns, thinking strategically as well as critically and creatively, synthesising varied knowledge in studio and answering a brief with originality and systems thinking.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will be able to take complex proposals through to resolution with a clear method, synthesising diverse knowledge in studio, thinking strategically and in systems and answering briefs with originality as well as technical coherence.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will be able to take a complex design from first idea to a resolved scheme, with a clear method, drawing together many kinds of knowledge, thinking strategically and in systems and answering the brief with originality.

statements.about: sophisticated spatial and material expression
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to conceive, develop and express sophisticated spatial relationships and material qualities through drawing, modelling and making, evolving a considered architectural language that produces coherent, habitable spaces showing rigour and skill.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will be able to develop and articulate sophisticated spatial and material relationships through drawing, modelling and making, with a considered architectural language that yields coherent, habitable space.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will be able to develop and express rich spatial and material ideas through drawing, models and making, with an architectural language of your own that creates coherent spaces people can live in.

statements.about: cultural contexts, narratives and social and climate justice
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to understand and engage critically with the cultural, historical, theoretical, artistic and social settings of architecture, analysing narratives, values and precedents to inform design, grounded in global history and theory and in an understanding of social and climate justice.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will critically engage with architecture's cultural, historical, theoretical, artistic and social contexts, analyse narratives, values and precedents for design and understand social and climate justice.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will think critically about the cultural, historical, theoretical, artistic and social forces behind architecture, use stories, values and precedents from many cultures to inform your work and understand social and climate justice.

statements.about: understanding and applying climate principles in design
statements.paraphrase: Will understand the principles behind climate change, the loss of biodiversity, environmental impact at global scale and regenerative design, why responsible materials, energy efficiency, waste reduction and ethical sourcing matter and how to apply these principles to design projects.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand climate change, the loss of biodiversity, worldwide environmental impact and regenerative design and the importance of responsible materials, energy efficiency, waste reduction and ethical sourcing; they will apply these principles in design.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will understand climate change, biodiversity loss and global environmental impact, the strategies of regenerative design and why responsible materials, saving energy, cutting waste and ethical sourcing matter; you will apply them in your designs.

statements.about: understanding construction, building physics and life safety
statements.paraphrase: Will understand construction systems, building physics and pathology, materials and environmental technologies and their use in quantitative and qualitative design work, including the principles of protecting life, fire safety, access and inclusive design, so as to integrate strategies meeting suitable performance standards.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand construction systems, building physics, pathology, materials and environmental technologies, as well as the principles of life and fire safety, accessibility and inclusive design; they will integrate strategies that meet performance standards.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will understand how buildings are built and perform, the principles of life safety, fire safety, access and inclusive design and how to build these into designs that perform as they should, whether new, reused or conserved.

statements.about: applying digital tools, BIM and GenAI
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to apply digital tools and technologies effectively, and put them to work, in design, evaluation and communication, knowing how practice uses BIM, computational design, digital fabrication, virtual reality, generative AI and data security.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will apply digital tools effectively and put them to purposeful use in design, evaluation and communication, knowing how practice uses BIM, computation, digital fabrication, virtual reality, generative AI and data security.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will be able to use digital tools effectively and purposefully in designing, testing and presenting, and you will know how architects use BIM, computational design, digital fabrication, virtual reality and generative AI, and how they keep data secure.

statements.about: applying research methods to projects
statements.paraphrase: Will understand the research methods of architecture and their part in innovation-informed decisions and the growth of knowledge, and will be able to apply suitable research or enquiry methods to projects.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand architectural research methods and their role in innovation-led decisions and advancing knowledge, and will apply suitable research or enquiry methods to projects.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will understand how research works in architecture and be able to choose and use the right research or enquiry methods in your own projects.

statements.about: advocacy, civic responsibility and ethics
statements.paraphrase: Will understand professional codes of conduct and the principles of equity, diversity, inclusion and accessibility, together with advocacy, civic duty, climate justice, community engagement and the ethical effects of design decisions on society, environment and wellbeing.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand codes of conduct, the principles of equity, diversity, inclusion and accessibility, the principles of advocacy, civic responsibility, climate justice and community engagement and the ethical effects of design decisions.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will understand architects' codes of conduct and the principles of fairness, inclusion and access; you will also understand advocacy, civic responsibility, climate justice and community engagement and how design choices affect society, the environment and wellbeing.

statements.about: understanding the professional, legal and business context
statements.paraphrase: Will understand the principles of the professional, legal and business setting of architecture, including managing projects, procurement and contracts, policy, financial planning and cost control, planning systems, building codes and compliance with regulation.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand the principles of architecture's professional, legal and business context: project management, procurement, contracts, policy, financial planning, cost management, planning, building codes and regulation.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will understand how architecture works as a profession and a business, including managing projects, procurement, contracts, policy, budgets, the planning system, building regulations and compliance.

statements.about: economics, numeracy and project feasibility
statements.paraphrase: Will understand how financial and economic mechanisms, local and global, shape design proposals and the life of a project, with knowledge of core economic principles and the numeracy needed to judge business sustainability and feasibility.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand how local and global financial and economic forces shape proposals and project longevity, know core economic principles and have the numeracy to inform decisions on feasibility and business sustainability.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will understand how money and economics shape designs and how long projects last, know the core principles of economics and have the number skills to judge whether a project or practice is viable.

statements.about: emotional and social skills in collaborative design
statements.paraphrase: Will have the social ability to understand, read and work with others in order to design for them, including self-awareness, self-regulation and responsive skill in creative work, aiming to speak for others, build teams and improve shared wellbeing through community engagement.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will understand, interpret and collaborate with others to design for them, with self-awareness, self-regulation and skilled responsiveness, and will learn to speak up for others, form teams and raise shared wellbeing.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will be able to understand and work with others to design for them, knowing and managing yourself in creative work, standing up for others, building teams and improving wellbeing through work with communities.

statements.about: communicating complex ideas and critical documentation
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to put complex architectural ideas across clearly and effectively by spoken or other means, in writing and visually, presenting to varied audiences and producing coherent, critically informed documents that support critical thinking, design intent and professional practice.

forPractitioner.text: Every master's graduate will communicate complex architectural ideas clearly and effectively in verbal or non-verbal, written and visual forms, present to diverse audiences and produce coherent, critically informed documentation that serves design intent and practice.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's, at minimum, you will be able to explain complex architectural ideas clearly in speech or other forms, in writing and visually, present to different audiences and produce clear, critical documents that show your thinking, design intent and professional approach.
